title: How to read Revelation
hook: apocalypse means unveiling, not catastrophe; its images reveal who really rules

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great thinkers' long, unfinished table. Your line was join the conversation.

Zombies in the streets. Cities underwater. A lone survivor with a dog and a shotgun. When a movie poster says apocalypse, it's selling the end of everything. Yet the Bible's last book, which some call the Apocalypse, begins with a blessing, a greeting, grace and peace. There are strange beasts in it, yes: fire, trumpets, a dragon. But it isn't mainly about how the world ends. It's about what's really going on underneath. Back on Mark's little apocalypse, you heard that Christians read the end-time pictures in several ways. This path now reads it slowly, starting with the word on its front door.
screen: `A BOOK THAT OPENS WITH GRACE AND PEACE.`

segments.voice: In Greek, the book's very first word is apokalypsis: an uncovering, an unveiling, the cloth pulled off something that was there all along. The King James puts it: "The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass." A revelation, not a catastrophe. Second, what gets unveiled. John writes to churches, some under pressure, in a world where other powers looked like they owned everything. Revelation pulls back the curtain on another throne, in heaven, and the one who actually rules. One scene holds the key. John sees a sealed scroll and weeps, because no one can open it. An elder tells him: "Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book." John turns to see the lion, and sees "a Lamb as it had been slain." A lion announced; a wounded lamb appears. Some readers see the whole book in that turn: for them, power, unveiled, looks like self-giving love. Third, how Christians read it. Some mainly as a letter to churches in John's own day. Some as largely about the end of history. Some as a picture of every age. Churches weigh these readings differently, and some readers combine them. Fourth, the tone. Many readers find that, read slowly, it sounds like courage, not panic. Near its end it promises: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." That's where the unveiling is headed.

Let one line from the opening sit with you: "Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy." The book blesses whoever reads it, so if strange images or old fears about the end come up, let them pass like weather. If you pray, ask to see what's really there; if not, rest in the idea that something true might lie under the surface of today.
Apocalypse. From the Greek apokalypsis, an uncovering. Not the end of the world: the cloth pulled off, to show who really rules.
Your line: an unveiling. A word to open the book with, not to fear. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Christians read Revelation in different ways: some churches read it chiefly as a message to its first readers, some as prophecy of the end, and some as a picture for every age; its hymns are sung in worship across churches.
